items.quote: The River Liffey (historically An Ruirthe(a)ch) is a river in eastern Ireland that ultimately flows through the centre of Dublin
items.note: The Dodder and Tolka also flow through Dublin, but only the Liffey runs through the centre; 'centre' makes it single-answer.

items.quote: St. James's Gate Brewery is a brewery founded in 1759 in Dublin, Ireland, by Arthur Guinness
items.note: Same article: 'On 31 December, he signed a 9,000-year lease at £45 per annum for the unused brewery.' The lease is no longer in effect (the property was bought out), but the question is historical, so fine.

items.quote: has housed the Book of Kells since 1661
items.note: Rechecked after rewording; 'Ireland's most famous medieval manuscript' excludes the Book of Durrow (also a Trinity Gospel book). en:Book_of_Kells: 'It has been on display to the public in the Old Library at Trinity since the 19th century.' One answer.

items.quote: During the Easter Rising of 1916, the GPO served as the headquarters of the uprising's leaders.
Bloomsday (Irish, Lá Bloom), is a commemoration and celebration of the life of Irish writer James Joyce, observed annually in Dublin and elsewhere on 16 June.

items.note: Same sentence gives the literal sense as 'Blackpool'. Dubh also means 'dark', so accept 'dark pool' when marking.

items.quote: Croke Park is the association's flagship venue and is known colloquially as Croker or Headquarters, since the venue doubles as the association's base.
items.note: en:Croke_Park also says 'It is the headquarters of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA).'

items.quote: The Phoenix Park is a large public urban park in Dublin
items.note: Same article: 'since the 17th century has been home to a herd of wild fallow deer' and 'The residence of the president of Ireland, Áras an Uachtaráin, built in 1754, is located in the park.'

items.quote: Stoker was born on 8 November 1847 at 15 Marino Crescent, Clontarf, in Dublin, Ireland.
items.note: Same article: 'He was the author of the Gothic horror novel Dracula (1897)'.

items.quote: The folk song "Molly Malone" is also known as "Cockles and Mussels" because the title character's sale of the two foods is referred to in the song's refrain.
items.note: The lyrics in en:Molly_Malone sit inside a poem template the checker strips, hence this article. Minor: the song's alternative title is 'Cockles and Mussels', so the question half-gives itself away to anyone who knows the title.
